document.title: Toronto Notes 2025
document.subtitle: Comprehensive Medical Reference and Review for the MCCQE, 41st edition

questions.question: A 29-year-old woman reports irritability, low mood, breast tenderness and abdominal bloating beginning about 5 days before each period and resolving within 4 days of the onset of menses. Symptoms have been recorded prospectively over two cycles and are interfering with her work performance. She takes no medications and drinks no alcohol. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Estradiol patch 100 µg with micronized progesterone
Escitalopram 10 mg taken in the luteal phase
GnRH analogue with add-back hormone replacement therapy
Hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy plus HRT

questions.explanation: Her pattern of affective and somatic symptoms confined to the 5 days before menses, resolving within 4 days of flow, reproduced over prospective cycles, and causing occupational dysfunction meets the diagnostic criteria for premenstrual syndrome. First-line management per the RCOG treatment ladder includes exercise, cognitive behavioural therapy, vitamin B6, chasteberry, combined hormonal contraception, and continuous or luteal-phase low-dose SSRIs such as citalopram/escitalopram 10 mg.

optionExplanations.a: Estradiol patches with micronized progesterone (or an LNG-IUS) are second-line, used after first-line measures fail.
optionExplanations.c: Higher-dose SSRIs (20-40 mg) are a later step reserved for failure of low-dose therapy.
optionExplanations.d: GnRH analogues with add-back HRT sit near the bottom of the ladder because of hypoestrogenic effects.
optionExplanations.e: Surgery with HRT is the last resort, not an initial option for a treatment-naive patient.

questions.question: A 16-year-old girl has never had a menstrual period. She has no breast development and no pubic or axillary hair. Pelvic ultrasound shows a small uterus and streak-like gonads. Serum FSH is markedly elevated and prolactin and TSH are normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Primary amenorrhea is classified by the presence of secondary sexual development and by FSH level. Absent secondary sexual characteristics with a high FSH indicates hypergonadotropic hypogonadism, whose classic cause is gonadal dysgenesis (e.g. Turner's XO or normal 46XX/46XY karyotypes); it is also listed as the most common cause of primary amenorrhea overall.

optionExplanations.a: Müllerian agenesis presents with normal breast development but abnormal uterine development, not absent secondary sexual characteristics.
optionExplanations.b: Androgen insensitivity also falls in the normal-breast, abnormal-uterus group.
optionExplanations.d: Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea produces low, not high, gonadotropins.
optionExplanations.e: Kallmann syndrome is a hypogonadotropic (low FSH) cause of pituitary failure.

questions.question: A 17-year-old presents with recurrent crampy lower abdominal pain that starts a few hours before her menstrual flow and lasts about two days, radiating to her lower back and inner thighs, with nausea and fatigue. She has no dyspareunia, no intermenstrual bleeding, and is not sexually active. Physical examination is unremarkable. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Scheduled naproxen begun before the onset of menstrual pain
Codeine analgesia taken once pain becomes severe
Insertion of a levonorgestrel intrauterine system

questions.explanation: Recurrent crampy lower abdominal pain during menses in the absence of demonstrable disease, with prostaglandin-associated nausea and fatigue and no features of secondary dysmenorrhea, is primary dysmenorrhea. Treatment is regular exercise, local heat, and NSAIDs, which should be started before the onset of pain; combined hormonal contraceptives used continuously or in extended fashion are the other option.

optionExplanations.b: Waiting until pain is severe forfeits the benefit of NSAIDs, which work best when started before pain begins.
optionExplanations.c: Hormonal intrauterine therapy is not the described first-line approach for primary dysmenorrhea.
optionExplanations.d: GnRH agonists are reserved for secondary causes such as endometriosis, not uncomplicated primary dysmenorrhea.
optionExplanations.e: Surgery has no role in primary dysmenorrhea in an adolescent with a normal examination.

questions.question: A 30-year-old nulliparous woman has 3 years of worsening secondary dysmenorrhea, deep dyspareunia and cyclic dyschezia. Rectovaginal examination reveals tender nodularity of the uterosacral ligaments and a fixed retroverted uterus. Transvaginal ultrasound is reported as normal. Which investigation would establish a definitive diagnosis?

options.text: Laparoscopy with biopsy of visualised lesions

questions.explanation: Her cyclic pain, deep dyspareunia, dyschezia and uterosacral nodularity with fixed retroversion are classic for endometriosis. Definitive diagnosis rests on direct visualisation of typical lesions at laparoscopy (the gold standard) together with histology showing two or more of endometrial epithelium, glands, stroma, or hemosiderin-laden macrophages.

optionExplanations.a: CA-125 may be elevated in endometriosis but should not be used as a diagnostic test.
optionExplanations.c: Ultrasound can detect endometriomas and deep infiltrating disease but a normal scan does not exclude endometriosis and it is not definitive.
optionExplanations.d: Endometrial biopsy samples the uterine cavity and cannot diagnose ectopic endometrial implants.
optionExplanations.e: Hysterosalpingography assesses tubal patency, not peritoneal endometriotic implants.

questions.question: A 27-year-old woman has cyclic pelvic pain, secondary dysmenorrhea and deep dyspareunia consistent with endometriosis. She has no adnexal mass, no bowel obstruction, is not attempting conception, and has no contraindication to estrogen. Her pain persists despite regular naproxen. Which of the following is the most appropriate next treatment?
questions.explanation: Surgical confirmation is not required before beginning medical management of endometriosis, and medical suppression is the mainstay of therapy. First-line options are cyclic or continuous estrogen-progestin contraception, progestins (e.g. depot medroxyprogesterone or oral dienogest) or a levonorgestrel IUS, with NSAIDs for pain.

optionExplanations.b: GnRH agonists such as leuprolide are second line and require add-back to prevent bone loss and vasomotor effects.
optionExplanations.c: Danazol is rarely used because of androgenic side effects including weight gain, acne, hirsutism and voice change.
optionExplanations.d: Surgery is limited to failure of medical treatment or desire for definitive treatment.
optionExplanations.e: Hysterectomy with BSO is the definitive surgical option, inappropriate as the next step in a 27-year-old with untried hormonal therapy.

questions.question: A 34-year-old woman with heavy menstrual bleeding has a 7 cm intramural fibroid and hemoglobin of 92 g/L. She wishes to preserve fertility and is booked for myomectomy in three months. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment while she waits for surgery?
questions.explanation: A GnRH agonist such as leuprolide is often given for 3 months preoperatively in fibroid patients because it reduces bleeding, shrinks the fibroid and corrects anemia, raising the hemoglobin before surgery. This is the preferred bridging strategy for a woman with symptomatic fibroids and anemia awaiting myomectomy.

optionExplanations.b: Uterine artery embolization should not be considered in patients planning future pregnancies and carries a higher risk of surgical re-intervention.
optionExplanations.c: Endometrial ablation should not be performed in patients planning future pregnancies.
optionExplanations.d: Danazol is not the described preoperative agent for fibroid shrinkage and anemia correction.
optionExplanations.e: Iron alone treats the anemia but does not reduce bleeding or fibroid size before surgery.

questions.question: A 22-year-old woman taking a 28-day monophasic combined oral contraceptive realises she has missed three consecutive active pills during the third week of her pack. She had unprotected intercourse two days ago and does not wish to become pregnant. What is the most appropriate advice?

options.text: Take one pill now, continue daily to the end of the pack, then take the placebo pills as usual
Take one pill now, finish the active pills, skip the placebo and start the next pack immediately, with back-up contraception for 7 days and consideration of emergency contraception
Stop the pack, wait for a withdrawal bleed and start a new pack on the first day of bleeding
Take three pills now to catch up and continue the pack as scheduled without back-up
Continue the pack unchanged; no back-up contraception is needed after week two

questions.explanation: When three or more pills are missed during the second or third week, the patient should take one pill as soon as possible, continue one pill daily to the end of the pack, omit the placebo (or hormone-free interval) and start the next pack immediately. Back-up contraception is required for 7 days and emergency postcoital contraception may be necessary given recent intercourse.

optionExplanations.a: Taking the placebo week extends the hormone-free interval and risks ovulation after three missed pills.
optionExplanations.c: Deliberately inducing a withdrawal bleed prolongs the unprotected interval.
optionExplanations.d: Doubling up on pills is not the recommended regimen, and back-up contraception is still required.
optionExplanations.e: Back-up contraception for 7 days is needed when 3 or more pills are missed in the second or third week.

questions.question: A 34-year-old woman who smokes and had a deep vein thrombosis three years ago requests highly effective, reversible contraception. She also reports heavy, painful periods and does not want to conceive for at least five years. Her cervical swabs for gonorrhea and chlamydia are negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate contraceptive method?
questions.explanation: Intrauterine systems contain no estrogen, so they can be used in smokers and in women with hypertension or previous venous thromboembolism, and fertility returns rapidly after removal. The progesterone-releasing IUS decidualises the endometrium and is preferred over the copper device for a woman with heavy, painful periods.

optionExplanations.a: Estrogen-containing contraception is contraindicated after a prior thromboembolic event.
optionExplanations.b: The ring delivers ethinyl estradiol and carries the same estrogen-related thrombotic risk.
optionExplanations.c: The patch is also a combined estrogen-progestin method and is unsuitable after VTE.
optionExplanations.e: The copper IUS increases blood loss and duration of menses and causes dysmenorrhea, which would worsen her symptoms.

questions.question: A 25-year-old woman weighing 85 kg presents 96 hours after a single episode of unprotected intercourse on day 12 of her cycle. Her pregnancy test is negative and she has no genital tract infection. She would also like to begin an ongoing method of contraception the same day. Which option provides the most effective emergency contraception?

options.text: Insertion of a copper intrauterine device
Yuzpe method with combined oral contraceptive tablets
Immediate initiation of a combined oral contraceptive pill pack

questions.explanation: A postcoital copper IUD may be inserted up to 7 days after intercourse, is 99.9% effective with about a 1% failure rate, and simultaneously provides ongoing long-acting contraception. At 96 hours in a woman weighing 85 kg it is the most effective option available.

optionExplanations.b: Levonorgestrel is ideally given within 72 hours, loses efficacy with time, and is less effective above 75 kg and not recommended above 80 kg.
optionExplanations.c: The Yuzpe method is used within 72 hours, ideally within 24 hours, with efficacy falling markedly by 72 hours.
optionExplanations.d: Ulipristal can be used within 5 days but is less effective than the copper IUD and delays restarting combined contraception by 14 days.
optionExplanations.e: Starting a combined pill pack is not an emergency contraceptive regimen.

questions.question: A 27-year-old woman with 6 weeks of amenorrhea has right lower quadrant pain and light vaginal bleeding. She is hemodynamically stable. Serum β-hCG is 3200 mIU/mL and transvaginal ultrasound shows an empty uterus with a 2.5 cm right adnexal mass and no fetal heart activity. Renal, hepatic and hematologic investigations are normal and she is reliable for follow-up. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: Medical management is appropriate for an unruptured ectopic under 3.5 cm with no fetal heart rate, β-hCG below 5000, no hepatic, renal or hematologic disease, assured compliance and willingness to follow up — all of which she satisfies. Methotrexate is given as a one-time IM dose with β-hCG monitored on days 4 and 7 and then weekly.

optionExplanations.b: Salpingectomy is reserved for a damaged tube, ipsilateral recurrence, or when medical criteria are not met.
optionExplanations.c: Salpingostomy is a surgical option when the tube is salvageable but carries a 15% risk of persistent trophoblast; surgery is not required here.
optionExplanations.d: Expectant management applies only when β-hCG is low and declining.
optionExplanations.e: Laparotomy is reserved for hemodynamic instability or extensive prior abdominal surgery.

source.reference: GY22 — Algorithm for Suspected Ectopic Pregnancy

questions.question: A 37-year-old woman and her partner have had regular unprotected intercourse for 7 months without conceiving. She has regular cycles, no history of pelvic inflammatory disease, pelvic surgery, chemotherapy or recurrent pregnancy loss. Her partner has no relevant history. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure and advise trying for a further 5 months before any testing
Begin infertility investigation of both partners now
Investigate only the female partner after 2 years of trying
Refer directly for in vitro fertilization
Start empiric clomiphene citrate without investigation

questions.explanation: Investigations should begin after 1 year of regular unprotected intercourse in women under 35, after more than 6 months in those aged 35-40, and immediately in women over 40. At 37 with 7 months of trying she meets the threshold, and both members of the couple must be investigated.

optionExplanations.a: Waiting a further 5 months ignores the earlier threshold that applies between ages 35 and 40.
optionExplanations.c: Both partners must be investigated, and a 2-year delay is not supported at her age.
optionExplanations.d: Referral for assisted reproduction precedes no diagnostic workup; the cause has not yet been established.
optionExplanations.e: Ovulation induction is not appropriate before investigation, particularly as her cycles are regular.

source.reference: GY23 — Infertility: When Should Investigations Begin

questions.question: A 23-year-old woman reports having only five periods in the past year, increasing facial and chest hair, and acne. Her BMI is 32 kg/m2 and she has darkened skin folds in the axillae. Free testosterone is raised, while prolactin, TSH and 17-hydroxyprogesterone are normal. Pelvic ultrasound shows multiple small follicles in both ovaries. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The Rotterdam criteria require 2 of 3: oligomenorrhea or irregular menses, hyperandrogenism (clinical hirsutism or acne, or raised free testosterone), and polycystic ovaries on ultrasound. She fulfils all three, and acanthosis nigricans reflects the insulin resistance that accompanies PCOS.

optionExplanations.b: Late-onset congenital adrenal hyperplasia from 21-hydroxylase deficiency is excluded by a normal 17-hydroxyprogesterone.
optionExplanations.c: Cushing's syndrome is a mimic of PCOS but is not supported by these findings.
optionExplanations.d: Prolactin is normal, excluding hyperprolactinemia as the cause of her oligomenorrhea.
optionExplanations.e: Androgen-secreting neoplasms typically cause rapid virilization rather than this gradual picture with bilateral polycystic ovaries.

questions.question: A 32-year-old woman has a Pap test showing a high-grade abnormality, and colposcopically directed biopsy confirms HSIL (CIN II). The transformation zone was fully visualised, there is no lesion extending into the endocervical canal, and there is no suspicion of invasive disease. What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Excisional procedure such as LEEP or cold knife cone
Annual Pap tests by her primary care provider for 3 years

questions.explanation: For women 25 years and older with HSIL (CIN II/CIN III) on colposcopic histology, excisional procedures such as cold knife conization or LEEP, or laser, are the preferred management. Those with positive margins require follow-up colposcopy with directed biopsies and/or endocervical curettage.

optionExplanations.b: Repeat cytology alone leaves a high-grade precancerous lesion untreated.
optionExplanations.c: Six-monthly colposcopy for 2 years is an option offered to women under 25, not to a 32-year-old.
optionExplanations.d: Serial annual Paps by primary care apply to women under 25 with LSIL, ASCUS or normal cytology.
optionExplanations.e: Hysterectomy is not the treatment for HSIL; excision preserves the uterus and provides histology.

source.reference: GY50 — Management of Abnormal Cervical Histology

questions.question: A 19-year-old woman has 3 days of lower abdominal pain, purulent cervical discharge and a temperature of 38.6°C. Examination reveals cervical motion, uterine and right adnexal tenderness. Transvaginal ultrasound demonstrates a 5 cm tubo-ovarian abscess. She is not pregnant. What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Admission for intravenous cefoxitin plus doxycycline
Outpatient ceftriaxone 500 mg IM once plus doxycycline 100 mg PO BID for 14 days
Outpatient levofloxacin 500 mg PO daily for 14 days
Outpatient metronidazole 500 mg PO BID for 14 days alone
Oral azithromycin 1 g single dose with review in one week

questions.explanation: Her cervical motion, uterine and adnexal tenderness with fever above 38.3°C confirm pelvic inflammatory disease. An adnexal or tubo-ovarian mass or pelvic abscess is an indication for inpatient management, as are moderate to severe illness, pregnancy, an adolescent first episode and immunocompromise. Inpatient therapy is IV cefoxitin plus doxycycline (or clindamycin with gentamicin), continued for 24 hours after improvement then oral doxycycline with metronidazole to complete 14 days.

optionExplanations.b: Outpatient regimens are for typical findings and mild to moderate illness without a tubo-ovarian mass.
optionExplanations.c: Levofloxacin is a second-line outpatient regimen and does not address the need for admission.
optionExplanations.d: Metronidazole alone lacks the required polymicrobial coverage against C. trachomatis and N. gonorrhoeae.
optionExplanations.e: A single oral dose with delayed review is inadequate for a tubo-ovarian abscess.

source.reference: GY33 — Inpatient and Outpatient Management of PID

questions.question: A 53-year-old woman has had no menses for 18 months and reports frequent hot flushes, night sweats and disturbed sleep that have not improved with behavioural and lifestyle measures. She has no history of breast or endometrial cancer, thromboembolism or cardiovascular disease. What is the most appropriate initial treatment for her vasomotor symptoms?
questions.explanation: Absence of menses for one year defines menopause, and vasomotor instability is its cardinal symptom. Menopausal hormone therapy is first-line treatment for vasomotor instability, with SSRIs, venlafaxine, gabapentin, propranolol, clonidine, acupuncture and behavioural modification as alternatives. She has none of the contraindications that would preclude hormone therapy.

optionExplanations.b: Venlafaxine is an alternative for women who cannot or prefer not to take hormone therapy.
optionExplanations.c: Gabapentin is a non-hormonal alternative rather than first-line therapy.
optionExplanations.d: Clonidine is likewise a second-line non-hormonal option.
optionExplanations.e: Local estrogen treats urogenital atrophy and is recommended when that is the only indication; it does not control systemic vasomotor symptoms.

questions.question: A 52-year-old woman with an intact uterus, 2 years past her last menstrual period, has disabling hot flushes. She is free of breast and endometrial cancer, thromboembolism and coronary disease, and her 10-year cardiovascular risk is low. Her physician plans to start transdermal 17β-estradiol. Which additional step is most appropriate?

options.text: Add a progestin to the regimen
Continue estrogen alone and monitor endometrial thickness annually
Switch to low-dose vaginal estrogen only

questions.explanation: Progestin is given in combination with estrogen for patients with an intact uterus to prevent endometrial hyperplasia and cancer; endometrial hyperplasia and cancer are listed risks of estrogen-only regimens when the uterus is in situ. Hormone therapy is otherwise appropriate here because she is within 10 years of menopause, under 60, and free of contraindications.

optionExplanations.b: Surveillance does not prevent the hyperplasia and cancer risk created by unopposed estrogen.
optionExplanations.c: Local vaginal estrogen is recommended when vulvovaginal atrophy is the only indication and will not relieve disabling hot flushes.
optionExplanations.d: SSRIs are alternatives for women who cannot take hormone therapy, not an adjunct that protects the endometrium.
optionExplanations.e: Bisphosphonates address osteoporosis and confer no endometrial protection.

questions.question: A 64-year-old para 4 woman describes urinary frequency, urgency, nocturia and loss of urine when she coughs, along with a sensation of incomplete bladder emptying and two urinary tract infections this year. On examination with straining, a soft bulge protrudes from the anterior vaginal wall; the cervix remains high and the posterior wall is well supported. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Anterior vaginal wall prolapse, previously called cystocele, is protrusion of the bladder into the anterior vaginal wall and presents with frequency, urgency, nocturia, stress incontinence and incomplete bladder emptying with an associated increase in urinary tract infections. Her anterior wall bulge with a well-supported cervix and posterior wall fits this pattern.

optionExplanations.b: Posterior wall prolapse causes straining or digitation to evacuate stool and constipation rather than urinary symptoms.
optionExplanations.c: Uterine prolapse involves descent of the cervix and uterus, but her cervix remains high.
optionExplanations.d: Vault prolapse is an apical prolapse of the vaginal apex occurring after hysterectomy, which she has not had.
optionExplanations.e: Rectal prolapse is a protrusion through the anus, not a bulge of the anterior vaginal wall.

source.reference: GY40 — Types and Management of Pelvic Organ Prolapse

questions.question: A 64-year-old woman who is nulliparous, obese and has type 2 diabetes presents with painless vaginal bleeding 12 years after her last menstrual period. Her cervix appears normal on speculum examination. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an endometrial thickness of 12 mm with no adnexal mass. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Granulosa cell tumour of the ovary

questions.explanation: Postmenopausal bleeding is endometrial cancer until proven otherwise, and 95% of cases present with vaginal bleeding. An endometrial thickness above 5 mm is abnormal in a postmenopausal woman, and her obesity, diabetes and nulliparity are classic unopposed-estrogen risk factors for type I endometrial carcinoma.

optionExplanations.a: Atrophic change is a benign cause of bleeding but cannot be assumed with a thickened 12 mm endometrium and multiple risk factors.
optionExplanations.c: The cervix appears normal, and cervical carcinoma is less common than endometrial cancer in North America.
optionExplanations.d: Fibroids typically regress after menopause and cause heavy premenopausal bleeding rather than postmenopausal bleeding.
optionExplanations.e: An estrogen-producing granulosa cell tumour can cause postmenopausal bleeding but no adnexal mass is seen.

questions.question: A 5-year-old girl is brought to clinic with 3 weeks of vulvar irritation, pruritus and scant discharge. She has daily bubble baths, wears tight nylon tights, and uses no diapers. She has taken no antibiotics. Examination shows vulvar erythema with no ulceration, no vaginal bleeding and no visible foreign body, and there is no concern of sexual abuse. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Non-specific vulvovaginitis is responsible for 25-75% of vulvovaginitis in prepubertal patients and is the most common gynecological problem in this age group, not yeast. Predisposing factors include non-estrogenized thin mucosa, a more alkaline pH than in postmenarchal patients, poor hygiene, and irritation by bubble baths, shampoos and perfumed soaps. Treatment is enhanced hygiene and local measures such as white cotton underwear, sitz baths, avoiding bubble baths and avoiding tight-fitting clothes.

optionExplanations.b: Candida is expected in prepubertal children who are in diapers or on chronic antibiotics, neither of which applies here; the source stresses that the commonest prepubertal problem is non-specific vulvovaginitis, not yeast.
optionExplanations.c: Pinworms are a listed infectious cause but would typically be sought with a cellophane tape test; nothing here points to them over irritant, hygiene-related non-specific inflammation.
optionExplanations.d: Lichen sclerosis is a localized skin disorder producing white patches and thinning of the skin rather than simple vulvar erythema.
optionExplanations.e: A foreign body (most commonly toilet paper) is a recognised cause, but none was seen on examination and there is no purulent or bloody discharge to suggest one.

questions.question: A 26-year-old woman reports 1 week of yellow-green, malodourous, frothy vaginal discharge with dysuria, frequency and dyspareunia. Speculum examination shows petechiae on the vagina and cervix and an irritated, tender vulva. Vaginal pH is 4.5, and saline wet mount shows motile flagellated organisms with many WBCs. She is not pregnant and has one regular male partner. Which is the best initial treatment?

options.text: Metronidazole 2 g PO in a single dose
Fluconazole 150 mg PO in a single dose
Clindamycin 2% 5 g intravaginally at bedtime for 7 d

questions.explanation: Frothy yellow-green malodourous discharge, vaginal and cervical petechiae, and motile flagellated organisms with many WBCs on saline wet mount identify Trichomonas vaginalis. Treatment is metronidazole 2 g PO as a single dose, with metronidazole 500 mg BID x 7 d as an alternative, and trichomoniasis is treated even when asymptomatic. Because it is sexually transmitted, partner(s) must also be treated, and patients on metronidazole must be warned not to drink alcohol.

optionExplanations.b: Oral fluconazole treats candidiasis, which produces whitish 'cottage cheese' discharge with intense pruritus and hyphae and spores on KOH wet mount.
optionExplanations.c: Clotrimazole suppositories are an antifungal regimen for vulvovaginal candidiasis and have no activity against a flagellated protozoan.
optionExplanations.d: Intravaginal clindamycin is a bacterial vaginosis regimen; BV gives grey, thin, fishy-smelling discharge with clue cells and a paucity of WBCs, not petechiae and many WBCs.
optionExplanations.e: Boric acid suppositories are used as prophylaxis for recurrent candidal infection, not as treatment for trichomoniasis.

questions.question: A 19-year-old woman has 2 months of bloating, early satiety and increased abdominal girth. Imaging shows a large unilateral solid ovarian mass with no ascites. Surgical pathology after resection confirms a dysgerminoma. Her gynecologic oncologist plans chemotherapy and wants a serum tumour marker to follow her response to treatment. Which tumour marker is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Ovarian tumour markers are germ cell, epithelial or sex-cord stromal specific, and dysgerminoma produces LDH. Diagnosis of ovarian tumours requires surgical pathology, which here establishes the histology, so LDH is the marker used to follow disease.

optionExplanations.b: AFP is the marker of a yolk sac tumour (and, with β-hCG, of embryonal cell tumours), not dysgerminoma.
optionExplanations.c: Inhibin is the marker of granulosa cell tumours, a sex-cord stromal tumour.
optionExplanations.d: β-hCG is produced by choriocarcinoma and, together with AFP, by embryonal cell tumours.
optionExplanations.e: CA-125 marks serous and endometrioid epithelial cancers and has poor sensitivity and specificity, being elevated in general inflammatory states such as endometriosis.

questions.question: A 44-year-old woman describes 8 months of progressive hirsutism, deepening of her voice and recession of her front hairline, with infrequent menses. Bimanual examination reveals a firm, mobile 7 cm right adnexal mass. Serum androgens are markedly elevated, and there is no ascites or pleural effusion. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Sertoli-Leydig cell tumours are androgen-producing sex cord stromal tumours that cause virilizing effects: hirsutism, deep voice and recession of the front hairline. Elevated androgens can be measured as tumour markers, which fits this adnexal mass with rapidly progressive virilization.

optionExplanations.b: Granulosa-theca cell tumours are estrogen-producing, giving feminizing effects such as precocious puberty, menorrhagia or postmenopausal bleeding and a risk of endometrial cancer, with inhibin as the marker.
optionExplanations.c: Fibroma/thecoma arises from mature fibroblasts in ovarian stroma and is non-functioning, occasionally associated with Meig's syndrome of benign ovarian tumour, ascites and pleural effusion.
optionExplanations.d: Mucinous epithelial tumours are often multilocular, may reach enormous size and resemble endocervical epithelium; they are not hormonally virilizing.
optionExplanations.e: A Krukenberg tumour is a metastatic ovarian tumour, usually from the GI tract, with signet-ring cells, and does not typically produce androgens.

questions.question: A 41-year-old woman at 11 weeks gestational age by dates has vaginal bleeding and vomiting severe enough to need intravenous fluids. Blood pressure is 152/98 mmHg. Uterine size is large for dates and no fetal heart activity is detected. Quantitative β-hCG is far above the expected value for gestational age, and ultrasound shows a snowstorm appearance with bilateral theca lutein cysts. Which is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Normal intrauterine pregnancy with hyperemesis gravidarum

questions.explanation: A complete mole shows diffuse trophoblastic hyperplasia with no fetus, a snowstorm ultrasound appearance from swelling of villi, and theca lutein cysts due to β-hCG mimicking LH. Vaginal bleeding, uterine size large for dates, hyperemesis gravidarum, preeclampsia and quantitative β-hCG abnormally high for gestational age are its classic features, and hypertension developing before 20 wk should raise suspicion of gestational trophoblastic disease. Maternal age >40 yr is a recognised risk factor.

optionExplanations.b: An incomplete mole is associated with fetal tissue, shows focal trophoblastic hyperplasia with multiple echogenic regions and no theca lutein cysts, and presents much like a spontaneous or missed abortion.
optionExplanations.c: Missed abortion would not explain a uterus large for dates, β-hCG far above the expected value, or the snowstorm appearance with theca lutein cysts.
optionExplanations.d: Threatened abortion presents with first trimester bleeding but not with markedly excessive β-hCG, excessive uterine size or molar ultrasound features.
optionExplanations.e: Hyperemesis gravidarum with a normal pregnancy would not produce absent fetal heart activity, a snowstorm ultrasound pattern or theca lutein cysts.

questions.question: A 24-year-old woman requests termination of pregnancy. Ultrasound dates the pregnancy at 17 weeks gestational age. She is clinically well, has no bleeding disorder, takes no anticoagulants and has no IUD in situ. After counselling that included the option of carrying the pregnancy with or without adoption, she chooses a surgical rather than a medical approach. Which is the most appropriate procedure?

options.text: Manual vacuum aspiration with a handheld aspiration device
Suction dilatation and aspiration with curettage, without cervical preparation
Dilatation and evacuation after presurgical cervical preparation with laminaria tents
Medical induction of labour with misoprostol followed by oxytocin
Medical induction of labour with oxytocin alone

questions.explanation: For a surgical termination between 14 and 24 wk gestational age, dilatation and evacuation is the procedure used, and presurgical preparation of the cervix with laminaria tents is required. Pain during the procedure is mitigated with appropriate analgesia, sedation or anesthesia including paracervical blocks. Counselling should include future contraception and family planning services, and follow-up should be ensured.

optionExplanations.a: Manual vacuum aspiration with a handheld device is used up to 12 wk gestational age, well below this gestation.
optionExplanations.b: Suction dilatation and aspiration is a procedure for <14 wk gestational age, and at 14-24 wk cervical preparation is required rather than omitted.
optionExplanations.d: Medical induction of labour with misoprostol followed by oxytocin is an option at 14-24 wk, but it is a medical rather than the surgical approach she has chosen.
optionExplanations.e: Induction with oxytocin alone is not the described regimen; misoprostol is given first, and induction of labour is the only option after 24 wk gestational age.

questions.question: A 24-year-old woman presents with a sore on her vulva noticed 3 weeks after intercourse with a new partner. Examination shows a single painless ulcer on the labium majus with painless inguinal lymphadenopathy. She has no fever, rash or malaise, and no vesicles are seen. Initial serological testing for syphilis is negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Herpes simplex virus infection of the vulva

questions.explanation: Primary syphilis appears 3-4 wk after exposure (median incubation 21 d) as a painless chancre on the vulva, vagina, or cervix with painless inguinal lymphadenopathy, and at that stage serological tests are usually negative because the infection is still local. This patient's solitary painless ulcer, painless inguinal nodes and negative serology at 3 weeks fit that description exactly.

optionExplanations.b: Secondary syphilis occurs 2-6 mo after initial infection with malaise, anorexia, headache, diffuse lymphadenopathy, a generalized maculopapular rash on palms, soles, trunk and limbs, and condylomata lata; serological tests are usually positive by then.
optionExplanations.c: HSV of the vulva causes multiple, painful, shallow ulcerations with small vesicles, usually accompanied by inguinal lymphadenopathy, malaise and fever in a first infection, and prodromal tingling, burning and pruritus.
optionExplanations.d: Chancroid (Haemophilus ducreyi) accounts for less than 1% of genital ulcers, far fewer than HSV (70-80%) or primary syphilis (5%), so it is an unlikely explanation for this presentation.
optionExplanations.e: A vulvar gumma is a rare tertiary syphilis lesion consisting of nodules that enlarge, ulcerate and become necrotic, and it follows long-untreated infection rather than appearing 3 weeks after exposure.

questions.question: A 55-year-old woman has 3 months of heavy abnormal uterine bleeding and pelvic pressure. Her known uterine fibroids have enlarged rapidly over the past year, and she undergoes hysterectomy for presumed leiomyomata. Pathology of the myometrial tumour shows 15 mitoses per 10 high-power fields, tumour necrosis and marked cellular atypia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Leiomyosarcoma is distinguished histologically from leiomyoma by three features: increased mitotic count (10 mitoses/10 high-power fields), tumour necrosis, and cellular atypia. It is the most common type of uterine sarcoma, presents at an average age of 55 yr, often coexists with benign leiomyomata, and is suggested by enlarging fibroids in a peri- or postmenopausal patient. This specimen shows all three criteria, and the diagnosis is characteristically made postoperatively after the uterus is removed for presumed fibroids.

optionExplanations.b: Endometrial stromal sarcoma arises from endometrial stroma, is usually diagnosed by histology of endometrial biopsy or D&C, and carries a good prognosis; it is not defined by the mitotic count, necrosis and atypia used to separate leiomyosarcoma from leiomyoma.
optionExplanations.c: Undifferentiated sarcoma is rarer than leiomyosarcoma and shows severe nuclear pleomorphism with a lack of smooth muscle or endometrial stromal differentiation, whereas this tumour is a smooth muscle myometrial mass.
optionExplanations.d: Adenosarcoma is the rarest uterine sarcoma, a mixed tumour of low malignant potential containing benign epithelium with a malignant low-grade sarcoma, typically a polypoid mass in the uterine cavity.
optionExplanations.e: A benign leiomyoma lacks the increased mitotic count, tumour necrosis and cellular atypia that define leiomyosarcoma, and would not explain rapid enlargement with these histologic findings.
